subject: Banking
title: How Visa Actually Works
description: A short lesson to help you apply How Visa Actually Works.

hook.text: Visa processes 65,000 transactions per second but never holds your money. It is a messaging network, not a bank.

buildup.text: When you swipe, Visa routes a message from the merchant's bank to your bank asking: does this person have funds?

discovery.text: Your bank says yes or no in under two seconds. Visa earns a tiny fee for routing each message. Volume is everything.

twist.text: Visa never takes credit risk. If you default, your bank loses money. Visa already collected its routing fee.

climax.text: Visa is not a financial company. It is an information company. It sells speed, reliability, and network reach.

punchline.text: 65,000 messages per second. Visa moves data, not dollars.

quiz.question: What does Visa actually do in a card transaction?
options: Routes an authorization message between banks

details.summary: Visa operates a payment network that processes transactions between cardholders, merchants, issuing banks, and acquiring banks in roughly two seconds, but Visa itself never lends money or holds customer deposits.
details.whyItMatters: Visa's network processes over 200 billion transactions annually, making it one of the most critical pieces of global financial infrastructure. Understanding its four-party model explains who really pays for card payments.
takeaways: Visa is a network operator, not a bank or lender
Transactions involve the cardholder, merchant, issuing bank, and acquiring bank
Authorization, clearing, and settlement happen in separate steps

faq.question: If Visa does not lend money, how does it make money?
faq.answer: Visa charges fees for every transaction processed on its network, including data processing fees, international transaction fees, and service fees to banks. The sheer volume of transactions makes these small per-transaction fees enormously profitable.

faq.question: What happens in the two seconds when you tap your card?
faq.answer: Your card details go to the merchant's acquiring bank, then to Visa's network, then to your issuing bank, which checks your balance and approves or declines. The response travels back through the same chain in about two seconds.
